chapters.title: Yesterday’s money is not today’s business
chapters.short: Keep moving. Then earn the next sale.
chapters.intro: You have landed a deal. Good. Now keep your head. I want to show you why a healthy sales process keeps moving, and why the way you handle a customer’s money can matter as much as the original pitch.
chapters.takeaway: Keep the pipeline moving, and let customer trust come from something you actually do.
chapters.body:
I do not care how impressive yesterday’s deal was if it changes the way you work today. I have seen people make a little money, sit back, and start behaving as if the job is finished. It is not finished. I don't care what happened yesterday. It's over. You have to push forward at all times. Keep your reserves, appreciate what you have done, and get back to the work that brings the next customer through the door.

Now let me show you something I used to do when I sold advertising. I would sell a package for, say, 2,000. The customer would agree, the invoice would be paid, and I would call them again. I would say I wanted the campaign to work for both of us, because a good first campaign could become a long relationship. I would suggest waiting a week, perhaps two, rather than launching immediately, and I would send their money back.

“I do not want to sit on your money. We can still do the campaign. I want to get the timing right.”

Think about how unusual that feels from the buyer’s side. They have just paid, and the seller voluntarily lets go of the payment. When there is a genuine reason for that decision, it shows that the relationship matters beyond the next invoice. The action does more than another paragraph saying how trustworthy you are. You have given the customer something they can see.

I would come back with a larger opportunity, sometimes 3,000 instead of 2,000, while the smaller package was still an option. That is a different offer with a different price. The job is to make the extra value clear. You do not get to call it better merely because you want another thousand. The timing, the work, and the benefit have to stand up when the buyer asks what changed.

I used the same thinking with a 17 digital guide. A personal email matters here. If you simply press a refund button, the buyer might not notice what happened. Explain why you are returning the money, what will happen next, and whether the customer needs to do anything. If you say you are improving the guide, improve it. Trust is the useful part of this story. A made-up update throws that useful part away.

Then I might offer a real bundle for 40, including another product I had valued at 100. In another version I called the combined package worth 120. That is the offer. I still have to sell it, deliver it, and count how many people actually buy. Keep a simple record of whom you have contacted, what you promised, and what they bought. Be moderately organized. Be quick, but organized enough to deliver.

It can be easier to serve an existing willing buyer better than to find another buyer from scratch. Imagine 100 calls and only one person ready to purchase. You should take that relationship seriously. Make the next offer relevant, optional, and worth paying for. Do not confuse increasing order value with forcing every customer up a price ladder.

chapters.title: A definite is better than a maybe
chapters.short: Close the decision. Count the cash.
chapters.intro: I have tried waiting for people to decide, and I have tried asking them directly. I prefer a clear answer. But even a clear yes has another step after it: the money actually has to arrive.
chapters.takeaway: Give every lead a clear next step, and keep projected revenue separate from collected cash.
chapters.body:
A definite is better than a maybe.

Imagine you have ten possible customers. You can keep all ten floating around in your head, thinking they might buy tomorrow, or you can speak to them and find out where you stand. Get some definites. In my example, five buy and five do not. I would rather understand those decisions than build plans around ten maybes. This is about useful information as much as it is about a sale.

A clear close does not need a performance. Explain what you can offer, when you can do the work, what it costs, and ask whether they want to move ahead. If you have a real deadline or genuinely limited capacity, explain it. If they cannot proceed, accept that answer and agree whether a later conversation makes sense. Do not keep pretending a lead is active because you dislike hearing no.

Now here is the painful part. I once had what looked like a huge deal for my television advertising business. My brother had spoken to a junior marketing manager at a large food company. The idea was television sponsorship and advertising. The proposed deal was £600,000, with about £250,000 profit for us. We weren't rich then. A quarter of a million would have changed things.

I went to the meeting. The senior marketing person was there, along with the junior contact. They liked the presentation. They liked the advertising plan. I sent the contract; they agreed. We had emails confirming it and a signed agreement. In our heads, the deal was done. We were waiting for the money to show in the account.

Then the senior marketing person became ill and went on unexpected leave. The junior contact did not have the authority to push everything through. The managing director did not want to launch while the marketing head was away. So the invoice was not paid. We kept emailing. The payment never arrived.

I had already started thinking about what we could do with the money. Where we could go. What we could buy. How our lives would change. That is exactly the mistake. I had turned an expected result into an emotional fact. When it fell apart, I was furious and demotivated for about a week. I could not work properly because I was thinking about money I had never actually received.

Do not get excited about money until it's in the bank.

A signed agreement and available cash are different things. A proposal, a positive meeting, a contract, an invoice, and a paid invoice are different stages. Treat them differently. Understand who can authorize payment, who can stop it, and what happens if your main contact disappears. Otherwise you can win the presentation and still have no money to run the business.

chapters.title: Care mentally. Stay steady emotionally.
chapters.intro: If you take on more work, you will take on more problems. The useful skill is staying engaged without allowing every surprise to take control of your mood. I want your attention on the solution.
chapters.takeaway: Care enough to act, and stay calm enough to choose the next action.
chapters.body:
You need to learn to care about things mentally but not emotionally.

Think about what a service actually does. A cleaner removes a problem from someone else’s day. The customer no longer has to think about doing that work. You have accepted responsibility for it. You get paid, and now you need to make sure it happens. The larger the responsibility you accept, the more moving parts you may have to handle.

You have to be able to deal with stress. Things will go wrong. A website drops offline. A payment service blocks a transaction. Someone does not turn up. A customer needs an answer. If every one of these events sends you into a panic, a small problem can swallow the whole day. You will spend your energy being angry about the interruption instead of removing it.

There is another useless extreme: acting as if nothing matters. You shrug, leave the problem alone, and tell yourself it will probably be fine. That does not help either. I want the middle. You recognize that the issue matters. You understand that it needs a response. You keep enough control to think.

“The website is down.”
“Okay. I understand. What failed, and what can we get working first?”

That is the difference between taking something seriously and letting it take over. You can be focused without shouting. You can be urgent without making everyone around you confused. Your team needs you to turn a mess into a sequence of decisions: what happened, what it affects, who can help, and what happens next.

I am pushing you to become more capable of handling uncertainty. If the idea of another task makes you avoid every opportunity, you will keep the same small set of responsibilities forever. Start with work you can actually manage. Learn how to solve the problems that come with it. Your capacity can improve through experience, better systems, and people you can rely on.

Do not confuse that with running yourself into the ground. Exhaustion does not make a broken payment process more reliable. The point is to stay useful under pressure. Protect the attention that lets you make the next decision. Care about the outcome. Keep your head available for the work.

chapters.title: Sell the need before the object
chapters.short: The buyer cares about a reason.
chapters.intro: You can describe a product perfectly and still give the customer no reason to want it. I want you to connect what you sell to something the person already wants to do, solve, or change.
chapters.takeaway: Make the customer’s situation visible before you list the product’s features.
chapters.body:
You don't talk about the product. You talk about their need.

Take a pen. Someone says, “Sell me this pen,” and you start talking about blue ink, plastic, and durability. You have described an object. You have not explained why this person should take money out of their pocket for it. What do they need to write? An idea they do not want to forget? Notes for a meeting? Something they want to create?

Now the pen has a job. You are speaking about the buyer’s life instead of delivering a tiny manufacturing report. The same thing happens with a protein shake. It's the need that sells, not the product. The container is not the reason someone buys it. They have a goal, a routine, or a practical need they connect with the purchase. Your job is to understand that connection and explain it clearly.

Look at digital guides. I see people lead with page counts: eighteen pages, this many sections, this many files. Did someone wake up wanting eighteen pages? Probably not. They want to understand something or do something better. Explain that reason first. Then show what the guide includes so they can judge whether it will deliver.

Food gets sold this way too. A berry becomes a “superfood,” and suddenly people hear a reason to buy it. That shows the power of a message, but the message still needs to be true. Do not borrow a health promise because it sounds impressive. If you cannot support the benefit, you have not found a clever angle. You have found a claim you should not make.

Let us make it even simpler. You own a coffee shop. You can compete on price, make the room look attractive, and buy comfortable chairs. Those things may help. But think about the tired person walking past. What does that person want at that moment?

“Tired? Nice warm coffee.”

That is a reason to stop. You have connected a situation with an experience they can understand immediately. Compare it with announcing that you have beans in a cup. The first speaks to a person. The second describes stock. A useful benefit makes the object relevant.

You will catch yourself slipping back into product talk because you know the product so well. Keep returning to the buyer. Why does this matter today? What becomes easier after the purchase? What problem does it remove? Put the answer where the customer can see it. The object is still important, but it should carry a reason with it.

chapters.title: Make the relationship make sense
chapters.intro: I learned that a piece of paper does not put money into your account by itself. I also learned that sharing ownership is a serious decision. Look at what makes the relationship work before you depend on it.
chapters.takeaway: Use clear terms and aligned interests, and understand what each partner contributes.
chapters.body:
Go back to that unpaid advertising campaign. We had an agreement, and we still had a payment problem. What would it take to enforce it? Time. Money. Attention. Those are real costs for a small company. I was trying to keep a business moving, and a long dispute was not the same thing as a customer paying on time.

That is why I think so much about mutual interest. I want a relationship where doing the right thing continues to make sense for both sides. A supplier wants repeat orders. I want dependable supply. A customer wants the work done. I want a successful project and another order. Clear terms matter, but so does the reason each of us has to keep our part of the arrangement working. Mutual self-interest keeps the traffic of the world flowing. It keeps the business world flowing too.

Picture cars passing each other on a road. Each driver wants to avoid a crash. That shared interest supports a pattern of behavior. In business, look for the equivalent. What makes the other person want this to keep working? What do you give them that they value? What do they give you? Do not wait until there is a dispute before asking those questions.

Now think about partners. I knew someone in a service business with three owners. Each had roughly a third. Two of the owners combined their position and pushed the third person out. Roughly 33% each. Two together, roughly 66%. The lesson that stayed with me was that the relationship had reached a point where the other two did not think they needed him.

Make sure your partners need you and make sure you need your partners.

I am not saying you must do everything alone. I have worked with partners. A fifty-fifty arrangement can make sense when each person brings something important. One may sell while another can deliver. One may know the market while another can build the operation. You should be able to explain why the business is stronger with both of you.

But do you actually need to give away half the ownership because you want someone to discuss ideas with? You may need a good second-in-command, not another owner. A trusted senior employee can challenge your thinking and carry responsibility without the same ownership arrangement. Decide which relationship the work calls for.

Be clear about contribution, authority, and what happens if someone leaves. Do not manufacture dependence by hiding information from each other. That makes the whole business fragile. Build something where people have good reasons to cooperate and enough clarity to understand what they are agreeing to. The relationship should help the work happen, not become another problem you cannot explain.

chapters.title: Help them see the decision and the future
chapters.short: A purchase needs a next step.
chapters.intro: People may think for a long time before buying, but there is still a moment when they decide. I want you to make that moment clear and help them picture what using the purchase will look like.
chapters.takeaway: Connect a clear present decision to a realistic future the customer can understand.
chapters.body:
A person can research a house for months and still have a final moment when they say yes. That moment is what I am interested in. The need has become clear enough, the offer makes enough sense, and the person decides to move. If your sales conversation never reaches a decision, you can talk forever without finding out what the customer wants to do.

Think about an estate agent showing a house. The buyer sees the rooms and imagines living there. Information about other genuine viewings may affect the timing. The important word is genuine. Invented competition does not improve the property. It simply makes the decision less honest. Help the buyer understand what is available and what choosing it involves.

If I offer you a pen at the same terms forever, with no clear reason you need it now, you may leave it for later. That is understandable. You have other things to do. It is my job to make the reason for a purchase clear and ask whether you want to act. It is not your job to become excited because I have a pen to sell.

Now there is another part people miss. You should sell a future with your clients. Talk about how the relationship can develop. If you're talking about the future, then you've already assumed the present. Help the person see what happens after the first transaction. If we do this well, what could we work on next? What would they be able to do with what they have bought?

When I was trying to sell a small television campaign for about £19,000, I would discuss the possibility of much larger campaigns later. I might talk about a £500,000 campaign in two years, with program sponsorships and meetings directly with the channel. That was a possible future, not a promise that the customer’s budget would magically grow. I wanted them to imagine a continuing relationship instead of a single invoice.

The same idea works for a website. Build something useful now, and explain what a later integration could make possible if the business needs it. Or take a 17 guide: explain how the reader might apply it, notice a situation it describes, and come back with an example or a question. The purchase becomes part of a useful sequence.

Compare “If you buy this, you can read it” with a clear explanation of how it will be used. One stays stuck at the payment button. The other lets the customer picture the work after the purchase. Give them a future they can understand, then deliver the first step. Do not bury today’s actual terms under imaginary possibilities. The future should make the present clearer.

chapters.title: Sell the result. Look the part.
chapters.short: A specification is not the whole offer.
chapters.intro: I keep coming back to the same thing because it changes the way you present almost anything. Show the useful result, then make sure your own presentation supports the confidence you want a customer to have.
chapters.takeaway: Explain what changes for the buyer, and make your presentation support that promise.
chapters.body:
Sell the result of a product, not the product itself.

Let us stay with the digital guide for a moment. I can tell you that it arrives instantly, has eight pages, and contains 5,400 words. Those are details about the product. They may help you understand what you receive, but they do not explain why the subject matters to you. The result. Always sell the result. A person is buying help with something in their life, not collecting word counts.

In my example, the guide was about understanding dating and communication. That is the subject the reader cares about. Will it help them recognize a situation? Will it explain something they keep getting wrong? What can they learn to do differently? The result needs to be specific enough to understand and honest enough that the product can actually help deliver it.

Now look at the way you present yourself. Image affects the way people interpret a message. Clothes, the way you speak, whether you appear organized, whether the work looks considered: people notice those things before they know everything about your business. You cannot pretend that presentation has no effect simply because you know your product is good.

I had already made money in another business before I began selling information online. I had the house, the cars, and the visible lifestyle. That was part of the image people associated with me. Some people were more willing to listen because what they saw appeared to support what I was talking about. You should understand that mechanism without assuming expensive possessions prove anyone’s ability.

I am not telling you to blow all your money. I'm not saying blow all your money. There is a difference between presenting yourself well and buying things the business cannot support. A clear website, a useful example of your work, and a confident conversation may do more for your particular customer than a luxury car ever could.

Think about what your buyer needs to believe. If you sell design, they need to see judgment in the design. If you sell a service, they need to understand how you handle the work. If you teach something, they need a reason to trust your knowledge. Image should make the substance easier to recognize. It should not distract you from building the substance in the first place.

I do not want you hiding a useful offer behind a careless presentation. I also do not want you mistaking appearance for the offer. Get both working together. Show the result you can help with, explain the product clearly, and look ready to do the job you are asking someone to pay for.

figures.caption: Product details explain the package. A clear result explains why it matters.

chapters.title: Learn to speak so people stay with you
chapters.intro: I have sat through presentations with good products, good information, and a good price, then watched the delivery lose the room. Speaking is a skill you can work on. You do not have to copy my personality.
chapters.takeaway: Practice a clear, engaging delivery and give yourself thinking time without hiding uncertainty.
chapters.body:
So much of business is a person walking into a room and saying something. A meeting. A negotiation. A presentation. A conversation that decides whether the next bit of work happens. If you want people to understand your offer, get better at speaking about it. Learn to speak. It is a skill you can use across the whole business.

I have seen people bring a strong product and polished slides, then speak as if they are trying to put everyone to sleep. There is no energy in the explanation. They are describing something they know well, but they have forgotten to make it interesting for the person hearing it for the first time. You cannot expect a slide deck to carry the entire conversation for you.

My way of speaking suits my personality. I move my arms, raise my voice, and put a lot of energy into the explanation. You do not have to do it that way. I know people who are engaging because they are funny, positive, calm, or simply very clear. You have to develop your own type. Find a way of holding attention that belongs to you.

The next time you enjoy listening to someone, pay attention to why. Do they make the idea simple? Do they laugh and make you feel involved? Do they use a story at the right moment? Are they good at changing pace? You are already responding to those things. Start noticing them deliberately so you can improve your own conversations.

Here is a practical detail. People often fill thinking time with “uh” and “um” because they have not decided what to say yet. You can begin slowly, breathe, and let yourself form the sentence. You talk slowly. You breathe. You do not have to talk at my speed. Clear first. Faster later, if faster helps.

Suppose someone asks how a technical component works. You can panic and fill the gap, or you can calmly repeat the question in your answer: “I will explain how it works. Here is the part to look at.” You have created a moment to organize the explanation without pretending you did not hear the question. Then give a real answer.

Repeating the question is a small technique, not permission to bluff. If you need to check a detail, check it. The customer is better served by a clear explanation than by someone making up an answer at high speed. Practice speaking about what you actually know until you can make it understandable without hiding behind a pile of terminology.

Practice getting good at talking.

You can improve this in ordinary conversations. Speak with enough energy to show you care. Watch whether the other person is following. Remove unnecessary words. Learn where a pause helps. When the explanation becomes easier to follow, you have made the customer’s decision easier too.

chapters.title: The back end broke. Now what?
chapters.intro: Operational problems are going to happen. I want people around me who respond quickly and keep working toward a solution. A broken system should trigger a recovery plan, not an afternoon of staring at it.
chapters.takeaway: Build a controlled fallback, reconcile the records, and get the essential service working again.
chapters.body:
Everything will go wrong all the time.

That is how it can feel when you run the place. The thing that worked yesterday fails today. You fix one issue and discover another. This is why I keep talking about speed and stress tolerance together. You need to care enough to respond and stay calm enough to work out the order of the response. You need people around you who work quickly. You need teams which react to things quickly.

I used a bucket of water as an image for momentum. Swing it around quickly and the water stays in while it is moving. Slow down and the picture changes. I am using it to make one point: do not let a problem turn the whole business into a stationary object. Keep useful work moving while you deal with what is broken.

Imagine the order-management system fails while the payment system still works. That is a messy situation. You need to know what people have paid for and what you owe them. I have dealt with that kind of mess manually: finding transactions, checking dates and times, confirming what a customer bought, and getting the order back into the process.

“I paid, but I have not received the product.”
“I am sorry. Let us check the transaction and get the order sorted.”

You do not solve that by arguing with the customer. You confirm the record, explain the delay, and deliver what you owe. Send a free gift as an apology if it makes sense. That is useful only alongside actually fixing the order. A gift does not replace the thing someone paid for.

Be clear about the limits of the fallback. If you can track and fulfill orders safely while the main system is repaired, organize that work. If you cannot, do not create a bigger pile of untracked promises. Taking payment is an important function, but accurate records and dependable delivery are part of the same business. Get them working together.

The important attitude is ownership. Someone needs to say what will be fixed first, who is doing it, and how we will know it works again. Then go through the outstanding work one by one. Check that the payments match the orders. Check that the customers have answers. Do not leave the team guessing which pile matters most.

I do not want an excuse about the back end to become an excuse for doing nothing. There is usually still useful work you can do: answer people, verify records, repair the failure, and prepare the recovery. Keep the business moving through the problem with control. Speed helps when it shortens the mess. It does not help if it simply creates more of it.

chapters.title: Good people, bigger aims, clear confidence
chapters.short: Build the team and keep improving.
chapters.intro: I look for people I can rely on, not just names to fill a vacancy. I also want an ambitious direction and a confident explanation of what we do well. Those things affect the whole operation.
chapters.takeaway: Give dependable people useful work, aim beyond the current plateau, and know your strengths.
chapters.body:
Most people begin recruitment with a job title and then look for a person. I sometimes begin the other way around. I meet someone dependable, notice that they work well, and think about where they could contribute. If I believe I can count on them, I do not want to forget them just because I have not written the perfect vacancy yet.

The work is never done. Work is a black hole. There is usually real work waiting. Communication needs attention. Content needs to be written. Distribution needs someone to take responsibility. A useful person may begin with one of those jobs and later move into a more specialized role as the company grows. Look for contribution, not a way to keep someone busy. The role still needs to make sense for the business and the person doing it.

Now let me talk about where you are aiming. I want you to aim higher than the level you have already become comfortable with. Triple or quadruple your expectations. That is a way of pushing your thinking, not a financial forecast. If you never ask what more is possible, you can settle into a small result and stop improving the operation that produced it.

But do not become the person announcing a vast business before selling anything. There is a difference between an ambitious direction and an imaginary present. If you are doing 1,000 or 2,000 a day, you can be pleased with the progress and still ask what the next step requires. If you are doing nothing, your next step is not to invent a huge valuation. Your next step is useful work.

The same distinction applies to confidence. If I am paying someone to do an important job, I want them to explain the work with confidence. Think about seeing a surgeon. You want to feel that the person understands the procedure and has prepared for it. You do not want a vague performance that leaves you less certain than before the conversation began.

I used to go into advertising meetings and say we were the best at what we did. I would talk about our price point and the way we planned media. I was very confident, including at times when I had not done enough to prove the claim. That is the part to examine. Saying something strongly does not provide evidence for it.

Learn your actual strengths well enough to explain them smoothly. What can you do at this price? What do customers get? What examples show it? You should not sound apologetic for offering something useful. You should also be able to answer a reasonable question without covering the gap with a bigger claim.

Ambition gives you a direction. Dependable people help you move. Confidence helps you communicate what you can deliver. Keep all three connected to the work. Otherwise you can have a grand target, a busy team, and a bold speech while the actual business goes nowhere.

Understand what produced it and what limits it.
A larger target

chapters.title: Money moves. Make your contribution clear.
chapters.short: Find a useful place in the exchange.
chapters.intro: When I talk about money, I want you to picture a person choosing to pay. Then I want you to look inside your company and ask whether the knowledge needed to earn that payment is shared or trapped.
chapters.takeaway: Know why a customer pays, and make sure the business can keep delivering if one person leaves.
chapters.body:
A payment into your account comes from somewhere. There is a person or a business on the other side deciding to let go of that money. You are not going to stare at a business idea until currency appears. Someone needs a reason to pay you for something you provide. Why are they going to give you their money?

An old business partner explained it to me with water. The sea, the clouds, the rain, the river: water keeps moving. He said money is like that. If you stand in the right place when it moves, you get wet. I was about twenty, looking at a company with money coming through it, a large office, and new cars, even though the profit was not what it should have been. That image stayed with me.

The useful question is where you fit in an exchange. Plenty of businesses connect a buyer with a product or a service. They supply, arrange, distribute, or make something easier. That can be valuable work. But you need to know what you add and why someone would choose your part of the process.

“I have this. I am selling it to this person. They will give me their money because…”

Finish that thought properly. Do not give me a slogan. Give me reasons a buyer can understand. If you cannot explain why they should pay, you have found a problem in the offer. Work on that before hiding behind complicated language about the business.

Now look at the people who make that offer work. I have seen companies become dangerously dependent on an assistant who knows every password or a salesperson who carries the whole sales result. You are busy, so you let more and more knowledge sit with one person. Then that person leaves, and you discover how much of the company you no longer know how to operate.

We had an exceptional salesman in the advertising agency. He was better than the others. When he left, we suffered. What should I have done? I should have asked him to teach the others. Give the team a Friday morning session on the pitch, the questions, and the way he handled calls. Offer something fair in return: time off, additional pay, lunch, recognition, or another agreed reward.

Don't make anyone irreplaceable.

That does not mean treat people as disposable. It means do not make the business so fragile that one absence can stop it. Appreciate someone’s skill and spread what can be taught. Keep access organized. Document the work. Help colleagues become more capable. A strong person should make the team stronger around them, not become the only person who knows how anything works.

chapters.title: Real limits make a decision clearer
chapters.short: Availability and the reason for buying.
chapters.intro: I want you to notice how people react when something they want might not be available. I also want you to notice how weak a fake limit sounds. The useful work is understanding the need and explaining real availability.
chapters.takeaway: Ask what the buyer needs, check what is available, and make the next step clear.
chapters.body:
Imagine you sell a technical component. A customer calls and asks for two. Before you rush through the order, find out what they need them for and check whether you can actually supply them. Those are useful questions. You learn something about the buyer’s situation, and the buyer learns whether your offer fits.

“What do you need the two units for?”
“Let me check availability and get back to you.”

When someone explains why they want a thing, they have put the need into words. That can make the decision clearer for both of you. Perhaps they are ready to buy now. Perhaps they are only researching. Perhaps the thing they asked for will not solve the problem. Listen to the answer instead of treating the question as a pause before your pitch.

Say I can get two units. I come back to the customer and ask whether they want to purchase right away. Are you looking to purchase right away? That is a direct next step. If they say yes, you can explain the terms and complete the order. If they say next week, discuss what you can genuinely hold or promise. Do not claim stock is uncertain when you know it is not.

There is a reason I dislike the lazy digital version of scarcity. Someone has a file for sale and announces that the file is about to vanish forever. The customer knows a file can keep being copied. The message does not match the product. You have made the offer less believable while trying to make it more urgent.

In the 17-guide example, I considered whether limiting distribution might protect the usefulness of repeated material. Even there, the reason needs to stand up. A real limit can come from the work you can deliver, a date that matters, or an actual capacity constraint. Explain that limit plainly. Do not build an entire sales conversation around a clock that resets every time someone opens the page.

The point is to connect need, availability, and readiness. What does the person want? Can you supply it? What happens if they choose it now? Those questions are more useful than another vague promise that this is the last chance ever. You want the buyer to understand the decision, not regret being pushed into it.

A clear answer helps you too. You stop guessing whether this is an order, an inquiry, or a conversation for later. You can move the work into the right place and carry on with the next customer.

chapters.title: You have an idea. What have you done?
chapters.short: Action before another month of talking.
chapters.intro: I meet people who can explain what they want to build but have not taken the first step. I want to separate a real obstacle from the habit of waiting, then look at whether the idea has a commercial reason to exist.
chapters.takeaway: Turn the idea into a visible next action, and judge the business by demand as well as enthusiasm.
chapters.body:
I was talking to someone who wanted to start a makeup company. I asked why she did not already have one. She said she did not know what to do. So I gave her a simple outline: find suppliers, obtain samples, choose something worth selling, create the identity and website, find relevant people who could help introduce it, and begin selling.

There is work inside every one of those steps. You need to understand what you are putting your name on, whether you can supply it properly, and what you can honestly say about it. But an outline gives you a direction. You can do the first piece of work instead of waiting for the whole company to arrive fully formed.

A week later, I asked how it was going. Nothing had happened. Seven days had passed and she had not moved. That was the part that frustrated me. We could have been talking about samples she had looked at, questions she had found, or a supplier who had replied. Instead we were still talking about wanting a company.

I see the same thing with information products. Someone has an idea for a guide or a course. A month later, they are still “working on the idea.” What work? What has changed? Have they written anything? Have they spoken to a potential buyer? Have they made a first version that someone can examine? An idea becomes useful when it starts producing evidence.

Too much waiting, too much talking, not enough f*cking action.

I came up with this whole project roughly thirty-two to thirty-four hours before we started. By then we had made an advert, built a website, started taking enrollments, and were recording the material. That is how quickly I wanted things to move. Your project may have different requirements, but you can still ask what useful part could be done today.

Do not turn the need for investment into a reason to avoid every action. Earlier, I explained why I like low-cost starts and getting a real offer in front of people before building a huge cost base. If you cannot do the expensive version, ask what you can learn without it. Find the next piece of work you can actually complete. You already have the idea. Go. Stop waiting.

Now another question: why are you running this business? I care about the commercial result. People tell you to choose only a business you feel passionate about. Passion can help you stay interested, but it does not make customers appear. You need something people want and a way to deliver it at economics that make sense.

A business selling concrete can be commercially strong even if concrete is not an exciting personal hobby. It doesn't matter what you sell. It matters that it sells. A product does not have to be glamorous to solve an important problem. I used makeup as another example because my interest was in how the business worked, rather than in wearing the product myself.

You still need the right knowledge in the operation. Learn what the customer expects, find people who understand the product, and make sure the offer works. The point is that selling and operating skills can transfer. Do not reject an ordinary useful business because it does not look exciting, and do not assume an exciting idea is a business merely because you love talking about it.

chapters.title: Attention needs a purpose
chapters.short: Choose the conversation and show real activity.
chapters.intro: I do not want to spend my day in pointless arguments online. If I engage publicly, I want to know what it is supposed to achieve. Then I want real evidence that helps the right people understand the offer.
chapters.takeaway: Have a clear objective for attention, and use genuine social proof rather than manufactured urgency.
chapters.body:
I see people selling digital products spend all day fighting with other people in the same space. They get attention, but what is the attention supposed to do? Is the goal to bring relevant buyers to the offer? Is it just to get replies? Are they trying to damage someone else’s reputation because they have forgotten what business they are actually in?

Have a clear end goal. Have a clear objective. Before I enter a public argument, I want an objective. I did not bother with tiny accounts. I looked for more than 10,000 followers. That was a rule I used for deciding whether the attention could even be worth my time. The number alone does not make the argument useful. You still have to think about the people watching and the result you want.

I once criticized a popular film series and drew a large audience into the conversation. My commercial objective was to introduce a dating course to people I thought might be interested in it. I was trying to be provocative and humorous enough that some of the attention would become curiosity about the offer. I think I did around 15,000 in sales that weekend. That is from memory. I cannot trace every sale back to the argument.

The point is not to start attacking people because you want traffic. The point is to stop confusing activity with a useful outcome. An argument can cost time, distract the team, and harm the way people view the business. If it has no clear connection to a result worth pursuing, leave it alone and do the work that does.

Now look at a quieter way of influencing a decision: showing that other people are already choosing the offer. A person may be unsure whether your business is real or whether their idea makes sense. Relevant examples can help them understand that they are not the first person to consider it.

With advertising clients, I would talk about other campaigns and the work we were doing. I might mention fifteen people signing up in the previous two weeks. I would talk about holiday campaigns being planned well in advance. Those conversations made the potential client think about what competitors were doing and whether their own planning was late.

But the activity you describe needs to be real. If it is March, explain an actual planning schedule; do not simply claim everyone else is already ahead. A useful example helps someone understand the market. An invented busy season just borrows urgency from a story you cannot support.

I also used a website notification showing purchases. That can make a quiet digital page feel like a business people actually use. It should represent real purchases, not fictional names or a counter designed to make the visitor nervous. Proof works because something happened. Keep that connection intact.

People look at what others do. That does not mean you must pressure every visitor with a crowd. Give them accurate examples, useful context, and a clear offer. Let the evidence support the decision instead of trying to replace their judgment.

chapters.title: Find the new need inside the disruption
chapters.short: A changed market can need a new connection.
chapters.intro: When something goes wrong, fix the immediate problem. Then look at what the change has created. There may be a new need you can solve, sometimes simply by connecting people who already need each other.
chapters.takeaway: Look for the unmet need, the capable supplier, and a fair way to bring them together.
chapters.body:
A problem inside your business is unpleasant, but it can force you to look at the operation differently. Suppose your order system is missing information. You need to repair the records and speak with the affected customers. You may also find an opportunity to restart a relationship with a useful offer once you know what actually happened.

I used a face-cream promotion as an example: something normally priced at 10.99 offered for 0.99 when bought with another product. Even a break-even offer might bring customers back and create another useful interaction. But be clear about what it can do. A fresh order does not magically recreate every old record. Fix the missing information properly, and make the new offer stand on its own terms.

The bigger opportunity can be outside your company. A whole market changes, and people who were comfortable yesterday suddenly need help. The question becomes: what do they need now, who can provide it, and can I help bring those pieces together? That is the job: you have to find a way to identify it, one way or another.

Imagine an airline facing widespread disruption after a major attack. Planes are grounded, passengers cannot travel, and some people are stuck for days. If I were thinking about a later ticket offer, I would ask whether an insurer could provide an optional product that addresses interruption, refunds, or accommodation. I would not need to become an insurance company myself. I would need a real provider and clear terms for what the cover does.

That is one way I would look at a changed need. The passenger who remembers being stranded for four days may care about a protection option they previously ignored. The value comes from addressing that problem properly, not from celebrating the disruption.

Now take creators who earn from advertising on a large video platform. Suppose the advertising income falls sharply while the audience remains. The creators still have people watching, but the revenue model has been damaged. They begin looking at merchandise, and many do not yet have production and fulfillment organized.

If I were one of those creators, I could contact a merchandise supplier. I might say: I want to make my own merchandise, and I know ten other creators who need the same thing. If I introduce them, can we agree a commission on the business I bring? In my example, I asked for 5% of their turnover. That is a proposed arrangement to negotiate, not money that appears just because I made a call.

Then I speak to the creators and explain the service. The supplier gets customers. The creators get a way to sell merchandise. I get paid for a useful introduction if we have agreed it and sales happen. Make the arrangement clear to the people involved and make sure the supplier can do the work.

Find it every time.

What I want you to find is the opening for useful work. It may not require stock, a factory, or a new office. It may require understanding a problem, knowing the right people, and organizing a sensible agreement. When the situation changes, look again at where value is missing.

chapters.title: Look through the buyer’s eyes
chapters.short: Your specialist detail may be invisible.
chapters.intro: I can understand every detail of my own offer and still fail to explain why someone should buy it. I want you to step outside your own knowledge, then let a candid non-specialist show you what is unclear.
chapters.takeaway: Explain the difference a buyer can recognize, and listen carefully to the reasons someone would not buy.
chapters.body:
Let me draw the transaction as simply as possible. There is a customer. The customer has money. There is you. The customer decides to give you some of that money. That decision is the part you need to understand. You cannot stay inside your own head and assume the other person sees the offer the same way you do.

Take a massage business. You say your oil is the best, and that is why the session costs more. You know the oils. You know the supplier. You care about the difference. But does the buyer know? Have they ever noticed the difference? Have you explained a benefit they can understand, or have you simply announced that your ingredients are expensive?

Now the customer compares you with someone charging twenty less. As far as they can see, both people offer a massage. The visible difference is the price. I have told you not to build everything around being cheapest, but that does not remove your responsibility to explain a premium. If the difference is invisible, you have not finished presenting the offer.

You have choices. Explain a genuine benefit the customer can recognize, or stop spending money on a difference that adds nothing they value. Do not invent a medical promise because you want the expensive oil to sound important. Explain what you can actually stand behind. Show it in the way the service works, the information you provide, and the questions you answer.

Go back to a coffee shop. A person may choose it because the room looks warm, the chairs feel comfortable, the staff are welcoming, or it is easy to stop there. The lighting, the cups, and the feel of the place can matter. I want you thinking at that level: why would someone walk past and decide to come inside? Why you and not someone else? Why this shop rather than another one?

never assume the buyer has knowledge.

Even someone who uses a service often may not understand your categories. I had been getting massages for years because of training, and I could still be unsure about the difference between the types on the menu. Familiarity with buying does not make someone an expert in supplying. Explain the choice without making them feel foolish for asking.

Now here is a simple way to hear where your explanation fails. Talk to someone outside the business who will be candid with you. I used my mother for this. She did not share my specialist knowledge, and she wanted me to do well. She would ask the question I had skipped because I thought the answer was obvious.

“I am opening a massage business.”
“How much will it cost?”
“That sounds expensive. What makes it different?”

There is your first problem to solve. Then she might say she does not have time. Can you offer a service that comes to the customer, if that fits the business? She might ask how she books. Is the process clear, or have you made it harder than it needs to be? I used the example of a flyer and booking by text because the next step was easy to understand.

Ask why they would buy and why they would not. Write the answers down. The reasons they would buy may become useful points in the message. The reasons they would not buy show you friction to remove or a difference you have not explained. Then test those ideas with the people you actually want to serve. A parent’s opinion is a useful conversation, not the entire market.

I remember taking an expensive two-seat car to my mother’s house. I told her it cost around 300,000. She looked at it and asked why I would spend that much on something with only two seats. To me, the car had a value that was not about the number of passengers. To her, more money should buy more practical usefulness. We were looking at the same thing through completely different eyes.

That is the lesson. Do not become annoyed because a buyer does not share your definition of value. Understand the definition they are using. Sometimes you can explain the difference. Sometimes you discover the offer is wrong for them. Either answer is more useful than assuming everyone who does not buy has failed to understand your genius.

chapters.title: People need a reason to stay
chapters.short: Leadership, rewards, and the learning curve.
chapters.intro: I learned a painful lesson in a small advertising office: people can believe in a plan, but the operation still needs dependable leadership. Then I learned how much faster work becomes once the people and processes are already in place.
chapters.takeaway: Understand the whole reward people value, and build systems that improve with experience.
chapters.body:
Money matters to people. But if someone hates the job, dislikes the way they are treated, and sees no point in the work, a bigger number is not the whole answer. I want you to think about belonging, respect, progress, and the way the team experiences the day. Those things can make the difference between a place people tolerate and a place they want to help succeed.

After my first television advertising company, I started another one. I found an office for £400 a month. My brother and I sat there, determined to build something bigger. The earlier business had relied on people pitching directly by phone, which meant a lot of training. We had spent around two hours a day working on those calls.

For the next version, we divided the work differently. People researched marketing contacts and sent emails. When someone replied with interest, I handled the call because that was work I already knew. We looked for companies with several branches, because national advertising made more sense for them. A store-locator page could be a clue that a business had multiple locations. We also checked current contacts rather than trusting old lists that went out of date.

The advertised positions were commission-only, at 5%. On a £20,000 deal, the person would get £1,000. Two deals in a month would produce £2,000. Over time, people came and left, and we ended up with four workers plus the two of us: six people in the office. The four were doing a lot of the research and emailing.

Here is the uncomfortable detail. For the first solid month, most of them did not earn anything. They kept coming partly because of the future they believed we were building. I arrived with energy, talked about the replies we were getting, and tried to make the room feel as if we were moving toward something. I ordered pizza, around ten a day in the example, and we ate together while I talked about the plan.

Obviously, pay your staff well. That tells you something about leadership and community. It does not make food a substitute for paying people properly. Their time and work still mattered. If the only thing holding the arrangement together is a leader’s daily enthusiasm, you have not built a dependable operation.

I accepted a fight and went away to train for ten days. My brother came too. While we were away, all the workers quit. Every one. The leadership had disappeared, the room no longer had the same energy, and the promised future no longer felt close enough to justify what they were doing. The business fell apart.

I had built something that depended too heavily on us being there. Remember the point about not making one person irreplaceable? This is the leadership version of that problem. People needed a reason to believe in the work, but they also needed a sustainable arrangement and someone clearly responsible while we were absent.

I saw another version in a proposed sporting-event promotion. The people behind it planned to attract the best competitors by paying more. They had money, but they did not have the same exposure, camera quality, public platform, or prestige as other events. Some fighters preferred the opportunity to be seen and build their reputation elsewhere. The reward they valued was larger than the fee alone.

Now look at learning. When you've done something once, it's much quicker to do it again. Think about parallel parking. The first attempt takes attention and time. As you've done things, it becomes quicker to do things. With practice, the sequence becomes familiar. A website can work the same way. At first you find suppliers, recruit help, discover mistakes, and learn what you missed. Later you know who to call and what needs to be done.

I reached a point where I could ask different people in the team to handle different pieces, and we could get a new operation assembled in about six hours. That came from previous work, available people, and things we already knew how to do. It was not a miracle that a first-time founder should expect to copy tomorrow.

The early stage can feel slow because everything is new. Keep the learning. Write down the process. Improve the handoffs. Build the relationships. The problems change as you grow, but you do not have to solve the same beginner problem from nothing every time. Your next attempt can begin with what the last one taught you.

chapters.title: A slow period still needs a response
chapters.short: Understand the budget. Own the problem.
chapters.intro: When a customer says they cannot afford it, understand what that means. When the business slows down, understand what changed. Do not hide either question behind a convenient story and wait for the answer to arrive by itself.
chapters.takeaway: Understand real constraints, then give the problem an owner and a practical next action.
chapters.body:
A buyer’s money already has demands on it. Rent. Food. Transport. Something they have planned with friends. Something else they simply want more. When a person says they cannot afford your offer, you need to understand the situation rather than treating the sentence as a personal insult.

Sometimes the issue is value. The person has money for optional purchases but does not see enough reason to choose yours. Sometimes the issue really is affordability. There is no spare budget. Those are different situations. Explain the value clearly, and do not assume that confidence in your offer gives you a right to someone’s essential spending.

I used the example of someone selling supplies for gas and oil operations. Imagine a replacement pipe that costs money now but can reduce costs later. The buyer says it is too expensive. A useful answer would explain the actual saving, the conditions that make it possible, and what the buyer needs to compare. If the savings are real, the price alone is not the whole cost of the decision.

Do not just promise that everything will pay for itself. Show why the offer matters and what supports the explanation. The buyer still has to decide whether the timing and budget work. Your job is to make the choice easier to understand, not to turn a lack of money into a reason they must buy from you immediately.

I also talked about running an adult-entertainment business during a recession. There was still money coming into that operation while other companies were struggling. That experience made me question easy explanations that nobody was spending anything. People’s priorities did not disappear. Demand changed, and some things remained important to particular customers.

It does not follow that every business can ignore a recession or that every buyer can pay. The question I want you to ask is more useful: what does this customer still value, and have I explained the offer in a way that connects with it? Look at the actual behavior in your market instead of using a broad explanation to avoid examining the business.

Now let us turn that same attitude toward problems inside the company. Nothing fixes itself. Think about a flat tire. If you leave the car there and return a few months later, you do not expect the tire to have repaired itself. You know someone needs to do something. If you have a problem inside of your company or a problem making money, you better do something about it quickly.

I hear a business owner say it has been slow for a couple of months. I ask what they have done. They say they are thinking about placing more adverts. Months have passed, and they are only now considering a response. I would have been asking questions after a couple of slow days. Not because every daily change is a crisis, but because I want to understand what is happening while I can still act on it.

The same goes for a blocked payment service or a hosting problem. I have waited for providers to sort things out and found that waiting alone did not get the result. Follow up. Find out who owns the issue. Ask what is being done and when you should hear back. Keep the information clear enough that the next person can actually help you.

Inside the business, make the same move. If you lack customers, what can you do today to understand or change it? If the presentation is stale, what can you improve? If something technical is broken, who is repairing it? You may be able to test an inexpensive response rather than leave the whole problem untouched for another month.

My brother and I disagreed about this at times. In the adult-entertainment operation, we might have three or four quiet days. He would point out that there had been a large football match and customers had been busy. I wanted to look at the accounts, the presentation, the costumes, and the set. He would say it had only been three days. I would point out that a background had been the same for a year and start talking about changing the wallpaper and giving the room a different look.

That is where the conversation had reached: one of us explaining why a short dip might happen, the other pushing for something concrete to improve. Do not let an explanation become a reason to stop looking. Understand what the evidence supports, decide what useful work can be done, and keep responsibility for the next step clear.
